# Confidence Interval {#sec-confidence-interval}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Keywords:** confidence interval, coverage, t distribution, degrees of freedom
:::

The last chapter ended owing two numbers. Every band it drew was centered on $\mu$ and sized from $\sigma$, and getting either one means measuring all 10,000 students. A real study measures 20. This chapter builds the same kind of band out of those 20.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(68)

population = np.clip(np.round(rng.normal(70, 12, 10_000)), 0, 100)
our_sample = rng.choice(population, 20, replace=False)

rng_sim = np.random.default_rng(2024)
picked = np.array([rng_sim.choice(population.size, 20, replace=False)
                   for _ in range(5_000)])
means_20 = population[picked].mean(axis=1)

se = population.std() / np.sqrt(20)
truth = population.mean()
```

## Building a band around the estimate {#sec-building-a-band}

Go back to @fig-bands. We could plot that histogram only because we invented the 10,000 students and could sample them as often as we liked. In the real world nobody can. A study draws one sample and computes one mean, and that is the whole of it: a single number, with no histogram around it and no red line to measure from.

Your one mean is one of those 5,000. It came from that bell, even though you cannot see the bell.

And we do know two things about it. First, the bell sits centered on the true mean: that is unbiasedness from @sec-sample-is-not-population, which said the estimates scatter around the truth rather than to one side of it. Second, the bell's width is the standard error.

We will keep treating that width as known for now, exactly as the last chapter did, and come back to it.

So the shape we know for certain, the width we are borrowing, and the position we do not have at all. The position is set by $\mu$, and $\mu$ is the number we are trying to find.

"95% of sample means land within 2 standard errors of the true mean." That rule needs the true mean as its starting point: you stand at $\mu$ and measure outward. Without $\mu$ there is nowhere to stand.

Write that rule as an inequality and something becomes visible.

$$
P\left(\left| \bar{x} - \mu \right| \le 1.96 \times \text{SE}\right) = 0.95
$$

$P(\cdot)$ just means "how often the thing inside comes true", so the whole line reads: the gap between the estimate and the truth is at most 2 standard errors, 95% of the time.

The 95% is not what we need here. Look at what is inside the brackets.

$$
\left| \bar{x} - \mu \right| \le 1.96 \times \text{SE}
$$

Say that gap comes to 3 points, and your estimate is 73. Then the truth is 3 points away from 73, which puts it at either 70 or 76. You cannot tell which, and that is why a band has to go out in both directions: 73 plus or minus 3 covers 70 to 76, and the truth is somewhere in there.

Notice what just happened. The inequality never said which of the two numbers you start from, so we started from the one we have. Knowing the estimate is within 3 points of the truth is the same as knowing the truth is within 3 points of the estimate. The first version needs $\mu$ before you can use it. The second needs only $\bar{x}$.

So do it with our own numbers. The 20 students averaged 70.80, the standard error is 2.67 points, and 95% calls for 1.96 of them on each side.

$$
70.80 - 1.96 \times 2.67 = 65.57
\qquad\qquad
70.80 + 1.96 \times 2.67 = 76.03
$$

65.57 to 76.03. That range is a **confidence interval**, and its 95% is inherited straight from @sec-68-95-997, because it is the same inequality read from the other end.

The true mean is 69.99, so this one caught it. We only know that because we built the year group ourselves.

Now look at what went into it. The 70.80 came from our 20 students. The 2.67 did not: it is $11.94 / \sqrt{20}$, and 11.94 is the year's standard deviation, which takes 10,000 students to compute. A real study does not have $\sigma$, the 11.94. 


## What $s$ costs us {#sec-what-s-costs}

So replace it. Each sample computes its own standard error from its own spread, which means every interval now has its own width as well as its own center.

```{python}
#| label: s-varies
rng_sim = np.random.default_rng(2024)

picked = np.array([rng_sim.choice(population.size, 20, replace=False)
                   for _ in range(5_000)])
draws = population[picked]

means = draws.mean(axis=1)
s = draws.std(axis=1, ddof=1)
estimated_se = s / np.sqrt(20)

print(f"True sigma: {population.std():.2f}")
print(f"s across the 5,000 samples: "
      f"smallest {s.min():.2f}, median {np.median(s):.2f}, largest {s.max():.2f}")
```

Our own sample sat at 14.87, and it is not even close to the extremes. One of the 5,000 saw a spread of 5.61 and another saw 18.99, against the year's true 11.94. Run those through $1.96 \times s/\sqrt{20}$ and the intervals come out 4.92 points wide and 16.64 points wide, where the proper width is 10.47.

Build all 5,000 that way and count again.

```{python}
#| label: coverage-with-s
covered_sigma = np.abs(means - truth) <= 1.96 * se
covered_s = (means - 1.96 * estimated_se <= truth) & (truth <= means + 1.96 * estimated_se)

print(f"Using the true standard error: {covered_sigma.mean():.1%}")
print(f"Using s from each sample:      {covered_s.mean():.1%}")
```

95.1% becomes 93.2%. Nearly 2 intervals in every 100 that should have caught the truth did not.

```{python}
#| label: fig-intervals-s
#| fig-cap: "The first 40 intervals, each built from its own sample of 20 and its own $s$. The red line is the true mean. 5 of these 40 miss it, and the misses are short bars."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for i in range(40):
    color = "#adb5bd" if covered_s[i] else "#c92a2a"
    ax.plot([means[i] - 1.96 * estimated_se[i], means[i] + 1.96 * estimated_se[i]],
            [i, i], color=color, linewidth=2, solid_capstyle="butt")
    ax.plot(means[i], i, "o", color="#495057", markersize=3, zorder=3)

ax.axvline(truth, color="#c92a2a", linewidth=1.6, zorder=4)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("Score")
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

@fig-intervals-s shows where the losses come from. The bars are no longer the same length, and a bar that comes out short has less room to reach the line.

```{python}
#| label: who-misses
missed = ~covered_s

print(f"Median s among all 5,000 samples: {np.median(s):.2f}")
print(f"Median s among the {missed.sum()} that missed: {np.median(s[missed]):.2f}")
print(f"Share of misses with s below the median: {np.mean(s[missed] < np.median(s)):.0%}")
```

73% of the misses came from samples whose $s$ was on the low side. A sample that happens to look tight reports a small standard error, draws a narrow interval, and announces more precision than it has.

The samples with large $s$ cannot make up for it. They draw wide intervals that catch the truth easily, but an interval that was going to succeed anyway does not succeed twice.
